In our system, a lightweight global scheduler performs fast, SLO-safe, energy-aware placement using constant-time lookups from offline profiles and GPU state summaries. On each GPU, a phase-aware local scheduler continuously adapts task batching and compute resources to minimize power consumption. Festina further performs energy-aware workload consolidation to reduce GPUs' static power consumption via SLO-aware migration. Comparison with four SOTA LLM serving systems and one DVFS-augmented system demonstrates that Festina reduces energy consumption by up to 56% while maintaining parity in SLO attainment (within a 2% margin)
Container scheduling.comment: 13 pages body and 4 pages appendix, 19 pages total. Accepted to the 2026 ACM SIGOPS Annual Technical Conference (SIGOPS ATC 2026)

Container scheduling.title: Orrery: Modeling and Simulation of GPU-direct MPI Communication with SimGrid
Container scheduling.summary: Simulation of HPC applications is an essential tool for analyzing system design trade-offs and enabling effective hardware--software co-design. As modern supercomputers increasingly rely on GPU acceleration, MPI implementations have evolved to support GPU-aware communication, enabling direct GPU data transfers. Modeling these mechanisms is therefore critical for simulating HPC applications on current systems. In this paper, we introduce Orrery, an interposition layer built on SimGrid's SMPI to model GPU-aware MPI communication using existing collective implementations and flow-based simulation. Orrery intercepts GPU memory allocations, kernel launches, data transfers, and MPI operations, and models their execution in SimGrid according to target system specifications, enabling simulation without requiring physical GPUs. We validate Orrery using CUDA-aware MPI microbenchmarks and a Jacobi solver on up to 32 nodes of the MUSICA supercomputer and demonstrate that it reproduces key GPU-aware MPI mechanisms.
Container scheduling.comment: Accepted as a short paper at the PMBS 2026 workshop (held in conjunction with SC26)

Container scheduling.title: Revisiting Cauchy-Schwarz Norm Bounds for SDC Detection in LLM Inference
Container scheduling.summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) execute billions of floating-point operations per output token across many hardware accelerators. At this scale, hardware-induced faults can bypass system-level detection mechanisms and cause Silent Data Corruption (SDC). Algorithm-Based Fault Tolerance (ABFT) is the state-of-the-art technique for protecting matrix multiplication from such faults, but it incurs non-negligible computational overhead and requires thresholds to distinguish hardware-induced errors from floating-point roundoff. In this paper, we revisit Cauchy--Schwarz Norm Bounds (CSNB) as a low-overhead alternative for detecting SDC during LLM inference. We compare CSNB against ABFT through controlled fault injection and evaluate the runtime overhead of both verification and threshold determination across multiple model sizes, batch sizes, and generation lengths.
  Our results show that, on average, CSNB retains 99% of the fault detection capability of ABFT for the evaluated dense linear layers while reducing verification overhead by 87% and threshold determination overhead by 67%. For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router gate computations, however, CSNB retains only 55% of the fault detection capability of ABFT. These findings suggest that CSNB is a promising low-overhead alternative for protecting dense linear layers in LLM inference, while checksum-based verification remains preferable for the evaluated MoE router gate.

Container scheduling.title: Tremulant: Latency in Serverless Platforms beyond the 99th Percentile
Container scheduling.summary:
Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) increases developer productivity by removing operational concerns such as managing hardware and software runtimes. Because function instances are started on demand, some requests must wait for a new instance, called a cold start. These are a common obstacle to more widespread adoption of FaaS, as they lead to unpredictable latency spikes that are not acceptable for some use cases. To solve this, many cold start optimizations have been implemented.
  However, comparatively little attention has been directed towards the slowest warm starts. With improvements in cold start times, slow warm starts emerge as a new problem for extreme tail events. By analyzing a dataset of several million requests across seven FaaS platforms, we show that the long tail of slow warm starts can be hundreds of times slower than their median performance, while a virtual machine we use as a baseline is substantially more consistent. We confirm this across four independent public datasets spanning 2020 to 2025, so the effect is neither new nor specific to one platform. Moreover, the warm share among the slowest calls starts to rise again at the highest percentiles: the most extreme latencies are not only cold starts, and cold-start mitigation alone cannot remove them.

Container scheduling.title: Flex: Grid-Responsive Provisioning and Scheduling for Elastic Cloud Clusters
Container scheduling.summary:
Computing energy demand and grid capacity growth are at a crossroads. Data centers are becoming large, concentrated electricity consumers just as power grids face capacity shortages while also integrating more variable renewable generation, causing grid conditions to change significantly across hours and seasons. These variations create an opportunity for \emph{grid-responsive} operations, in which workloads are shifted to align energy use with time-varying grid conditions, prioritizing clean, low-cost periods of surplus generation and low congestion. Fortunately, a significant fraction of computing demand comes from batch jobs that are delay-tolerant and elastic, enabling clusters to shift or scale jobs, or adjust the provisioned capacity in response to grid conditions. However, provisioning and scheduling decisions are closely coupled. Effective cluster capacity depends on how jobs are scaled, while job-scaling decisions depend on the available capacity. At the same time, exogenous grid signals (\eg carbon intensity and electricity prices) determine the cost of both scheduling and provisioning decisions.
  To address this problem, we present \Flex, a grid-responsive resource manager for elastic cloud clusters that coordinates provisioning of cluster capacity and scheduling of elastic batch jobs. Flex takes a data-driven approach, periodically learning optimal scheduling and provisioning decisions based on recent history and reusing them to guide coherent runtime provisioning and scheduling. We implement Flex on top of AWS ParallelCluster and evaluate it using real-world workload traces and grid signals, including carbon intensity and electricity prices. Our results show that Flex reduces carbon emissions by up to $\sim$57\%, within 2.1\% of the oracle, and electricity costs by up to 60\% relative to signal-agnostic baselines.
Container scheduling.comment: Full technical report for ACM SoCC 2026 paper with a small name change

Container scheduling.title: FastEEP: Fast Intra-Instance Elastic Scaling for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving
Container scheduling.summary:
Large-scale expert parallelism (EP) has become the standard deployment configuration for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models in production. Meanwhile, the highly dynamic nature of LLM workloads requires providers to continuously adjust serving capacity to match fluctuating demand. Scaling MoE serving cannot be efficiently achieved by simply adding or removing serving instances; instead, it often requires resizing the EP group within an existing instance, which we refer to as intra-instance scaling.Existing inference engines primarily rely on instance-level scaling, which destroys and reconstructs entire serving instances, incurring substantial scaling overhead.
  We present FastEEP (Fast Elastic Expert Parallel), a fast intra-instance scaling system for MoE serving based on the principle of Partial Reuse. FastEEP reuses existing runtime state across worker execution, GPU memory, and communication by separating reusable execution structures from the resources activated by the current EP configuration. This separation enables coordinated resource reclamation and reconfiguration while preserving costly-to-reconstruct state, allowing fast EP scaling without full instance teardown and reconstruction. Our evaluation shows that FastEEP achieves 4.5x--11.7x faster scaling than the existing vLLM-based approach across different models, enabling efficient, fine-grained scaling of MoE serving.

Container scheduling.title: Dynamic Resource Management in Production HPC Clusters
Container scheduling.summary: Many large-scale scientific applications exhibit time-varying behavior, yet production HPC clusters still rely on rigid, fixed-size allocations, and most dynamic techniques remain confined to laboratory prototypes. This work presents a practical MPI malleability methodology that integrates with state-of-the-art high-performance computing (HPC) software stacks and operational practices. The methodology is implemented in the Dynamic Management of Resources (DMR) framework and is designed to ease adoption by existing applications without requiring intrusive code changes or scheduler modifications. We evaluate our approach by integrating the DMR API into two large-scale scientific applications and deploying them on three TOP500 supercomputers under realistic production configurations. Our non-invasive malleability solution achieves performance comparable to static baselines in controlled environments while substantially reducing node-hour consumption for identical workloads. These results show that malleability can be effectively exploited on production systems using vanilla resource managers, lowering the barrier to adoption of dynamic resource management in HPC.

Container scheduling.title: LunaTP: Enabling Efficient and Scalable Tensor Product for Equivariant MLIPs
Container scheduling.summary: Equivariant machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise atomistic simulations with accuracy approaching that of quantum-mechanical calculations. However, the high computational cost of their core Clebsch--Gordan tensor product (CGTP) convolutions severely limits model scalability and efficiency. In this paper, we rethink the parallel execution of CGTP convolutions and introduce LunaTP. Built on node-centric execution, LunaTP exploits path-group parallelism and multi-level reuse to accelerate CGTP convolutions and higher-order derivative computation while preserving the underlying mathematical formulation. On an NVIDIA H100 GPU, LunaTP achieves kernel speedups of up to 250.0$\times$ over e3nn and 17.1$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. It also delivers end-to-end training throughput gains of up to 28.7$\times$ over e3nn and 3.11$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. Finally, LunaTP demonstrates scalability and robust performance across models, workload scales, and GPUs, delivering substantial acceleration for training and atomistic simulation with high-accuracy equivariant MLIPs.
Container scheduling.comment: 26 pages, 11 figures

Container scheduling.title: HULK: An Efficient Algorithm for Enabling Fast Bulk Bitwise Operations on Homomorphically Encrypted Data
Container scheduling.summary: A wide range of important cloud applications, e.g., database analytics, graph analytics, and genome analysis, spend a considerable amount of time performing bulk bitwise operations (e.g., AND, OR, XOR). These applications often operate on highly sensitive data, making data privacy a critical concern. Homomorphic encryption (HE) enables secure computation on encrypted data without requiring decryption, ensuring privacy in untrusted and shared environments. We analyze 13 end-to-end applications across three domains (healthcare, graph, and database analytics) and observe that bulk bitwise operations take 62-100% of the execution time of the healthcare and graph workloads. The key problem is that existing HE approaches perform them with high-latency homomorphic operations (e.g., multiplication or lookup tables) and significantly increase the data size. Our goal is to enable fast bulk bitwise operations on homomorphically encrypted data by designing an efficient HE algorithm that reduces the use of these costly operations. To this end, we propose HULK, which performs two key steps: (1) it constructs bulk bitwise operations using low-cost homomorphic additions, which compute the Hamming weight of the encrypted operand bits in every slot of a packed ciphertext without any homomorphic multiplication, and (2) it decodes the result of an AND, OR, or XOR from the Hamming weight with a single indicator polynomial, keeping the result in the standard encoding. Across 13 end-to-end applications in healthcare, graph, and database analytics, HULK improves performance over the arithmetic approach used by prior works by up to 7.26x (CPU) and 6.65x (GPU), and on average by 2.32x/1.78x/1.45x (CPU) and 2.08x/1.70x/1.51x (GPU) for healthcare/graph/database analytics. When we increase the reduction depth in a representative application, HULK's speedup grows to 10.10x over the state-of-the-art GPU baseline.
Container scheduling.comment: 24 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables. Code: https://github.com/CMU-SAFARI/HULK

Container scheduling.title: Fast and Flexible Spiking Network Simulations on Massively Distributed On-Chip Memory Accelerators
Container scheduling.summary: Studying brain function and dysfunction in spiking networks with realistic synaptic densities pushes simulation technology beyond its current limits. It requires simulations substantially faster than biological real-time to cover long model times and enable efficient iterative exploration, particularly when connectivity is plastic. The modelling community aspires to a $100\times$ speedup. Yet on conventional many-core systems this remains elusive, bounded by inter-node communication and memory access. So far, significant speedup has only been shown on a custom-built FPGA system. We demonstrate the potential of commercial systems with large distributed on-chip memory to accelerate brain research. To exploit the local SRAM, we introduce a group-based mapping and communication strategy tackling spike-routing challenges on massively distributed systems. On Graphcore IPUs, the cortical microcircuit runs at a record $22.7\times$ faster than biological real-time with negligible build times and a reusable compiled graph. By design, the algorithm makes no model- or hardware-specific assumptions, providing a general strategy for advancing neuronal simulation technology.

Container scheduling.title: No Truly Sublogarithmic-Round Algorithm for Distributed MIS in the LOCAL Model
Container scheduling.summary:
We prove that $o(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n})$-round randomized LOCAL algorithms find a maximal independent set (MIS) with subconstant probability on some input. This shows that the 40-year-old $O(\log n)$-round randomized CONGEST algorithm of Luby and Alon, Babai, and Itai is nearly optimal. Our lower bound improves upon the $Ω(\sqrt{\log n})$-round lower bound of Khoury and Schild and nearly closes the 20+ year-old gap between the $O(\log n)$-round algorithm and the $Ω(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}})$-round lower bound of Kuhn, Moscibroda, and Wattenhofer.
  To close this gap, one must show a lower bound for a graph that is not locally treelike. We do this by starting with a $D$-regular, $Θ(\log_D n)$-girth graph, with $D = Θ(\log n)$. Crucially, this is not our final graph. We obtain our hard instance by \emph{replacing} each vertex of this treelike graph with a clique on $n^c$ vertices for some constant $c \in (0,1)$. We then replace each edge with a bipartite Erdős--Rényi graph between the corresponding cliques, with each edge present independently with probability $1/2$.
  We analyze arbitrary LOCAL algorithms on our non-treelike hard instance with a novel round elimination approach. We describe algorithms that output a set of vertices in this graph using two metrics: their \emph{occupancy probability} and their \emph{conflict probability}. Our round elimination framework takes an $r$-round algorithm and produces an $(r-1)$-round algorithm where occupancy and conflict probabilities collectively slightly degrade, but individually can significantly improve or degrade. This round elimination result is obtained by exploiting the lack of large biclique complements in dense bipartite Erdős--Rényi graphs, which in turn allows us to bound the entropy of the output distribution for any independent set algorithm.
Container scheduling.comment: 34 pages, 2 figures. Abstract shortened due to arXiv requirements

Container scheduling.title: A Distributed View from a Single GPU: RankLens for Distributed Training
Container scheduling.summary:
Modern distributed training is costly to debug, tune, and analyze because faithful analysis often requires repeated target-scale executions. We observe that many analysis tasks depend on the original distributed execution path, but not on full all-rank execution. We present RankLens, a single-rank emulation system that runs one survivor rank on a single GPU while preserving the target job's distributed semantics. The survivor rank executes the original training program and performs real local computation. At communication boundaries, the system replaces real multi-rank communication with task-dependent semantics, selectively restoring recorded communication results and recorded or estimated completion timing while preserving the asynchronous dependencies required for analysis. This enables replay from real executions and supports analysis, debugging, and tuning with existing debuggers and performance analysis tools.
  We evaluate the system on DeepSpeed and Megatron-LM across 8-64-GPU target configurations. RankLens achieves 100% training-tensor communication-structure match, keeps emulation timing error below 5%, supports local anomaly reproduction and execution analysis, and reduces the resource requirement of these analyses from target-scale clusters to a single GPU.
Container scheduling.comment: 12pages, 9 figures

Container scheduling.title: Space-Time Parallel Direct Numerical Simulation of Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
Container scheduling.summary: Rayleigh-Bénard convection (RBC) is a model for turbulent flow and challenging to simulate by direct numerical simulation (DNS). Adequate resolution of all relevant length scales requires very fine grids in space and stability restrictions can dictate small step sizes. In this paper, we investigate the use of parallel spectral deferred correction (SDC) as a high-order time-stepping method to reduce wall-clock times of direct numerical simulation of RBC. Performance results on JUSUF (CPUs) and JUPITER (GPUs) with two different codes show parallel SDC can offer some concurrency along the temporal axis plus larger maximum stable time steps. Taken together, this allows for a reduction of wall-clock time required for simulations over one free-fall time by having to compute fewer steps and being able to mitigate the higher cost per time step through temporal parallelization.

Container scheduling.title: Quota-Based Aging for Prediction-Guided Scheduling in LLM Serving
Container scheduling.summary: Large language model (LLM) serving systems use token-level continuous batching to improve resource utilization, but heterogeneous response lengths complicate request scheduling. Prediction-guided short-first scheduling reduces average latency but can severely delay long requests, while unrestricted aging may over-promote delayed long requests under congestion. We propose Quota-Based Aging (QBA), a lightweight policy that combines predicted short-first admission with quota-bounded, debt-enforced promotion of aged predicted-long requests. We also use a reduced M/G/n queueing surrogate, calibrated from simulator traces, to explain first-order mean-latency trends. QBA is evaluated using a serving-aware event-driven simulator that models decode-priority batching, chunked prefill, token-budget constraints, and KV-cache-safe admission. We compare QBA with FCFS, predicted short-first, and aggressive aging under asymmetric prediction errors on synthetic and production-derived workloads. The evaluation considers queueing delay, throughput, utilization, and class-conditional tail performance. Results show that QBA provides a controllable middle ground between aggressive short-first prioritization and unrestricted aging, substantially reducing long-request tail latency while retaining much of the mean-latency benefit of prediction-guided scheduling.
Container scheduling.comment: 8 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for publication at the 45th IEEE International Performance, Computing, and Communications Conference (IPCCC 2026), Austin, TX, November 2026

Container scheduling.title: An Asynchronous Maximum Independent Set Algorithm by Myopic Luminous Robots on Grids
Container scheduling.summary: We consider the problem of constructing a maximum independent set with mobile myopic luminous robots on a grid network whose size is finite but unknown to the robots. In this setting, the robots enter the grid network one-by-one from a corner of the grid, and they eventually have to be disseminated on the grid nodes so that the occupied positions form a maximum independent set of the network. We assume that robots are asynchronous, anonymous, silent, and they execute the same distributed algorithm. In this paper, we propose two algorithms: The first one assumes the number of light colors of each robot is three and the visible range is two, but uses additional strong assumptions of port-numbering for each node. To delete this assumption, the second one assumes the number of light colors of each robot is seven and the visible range is three. In both algorithms, the number of movements is $O(n(L+l))$ steps where $n$ is the number of nodes and $L$ and $l$ are the grid dimensions.

Container scheduling.title: A Minimum Exact Disjunctive Basis for Two-Robot Solvability Profiles
Container scheduling.summary:
We completely characterize the solvability profiles of tasks for two autonomous mobile robots in the plane under variable disorientation, chirality, and rigid movements. The four standard capability models and the schedulers considered here have a known quotient order Q of thirteen computational classes. A task's solvability profile is the set of classes in which it is solvable, and is necessarily an upset of Q. We prove that every upset is realizable and construct a minimum exact disjunctive basis of thirteen concrete tasks.
  The basis contains one task for each principal upset. For every antichain of Q, the disjunction of the corresponding tasks has profile exactly equal to the union of their profiles. This exactness is not implied by the individual profiles: an algorithm may satisfy different disjuncts in different executions. We establish it by constructing, for every algorithm in each maximal class outside the target union, a single admissible fair execution violating all selected predicates simultaneously. Consequently, the realizable profiles form the entire finite distributive lattice Up(Q): there are exactly 54 profiles, counted by the antichain polynomial 1 + 13z + 24z^2 + 16z^3, and each has a canonical disjunctive representation using at most three principal tasks.
  We also identify six tasks whose solvability signatures recover every inclusion and incomparability in Q, and prove that six is minimum even among arbitrary separating tasks. Their profiles are precisely the principal upsets generated by the join-irreducible elements of Q. In contrast, any task family generating every profile by exact disjunctions must contain all thirteen principal profiles. Thus our exact disjunctive basis has minimum size and is unique at the profile level.
Container scheduling.comment: 100 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables

Container scheduling.title: PerCache: Predictive Hierarchical Cache for RAG Applications on Mobile Devices
Container scheduling.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become a de facto paradigm in various large language model (LLM)-driven applications on mobile devices, such as mobile assistants leveraging personal emails or meeting records. However, due to lengthy prompts and resource constraints, mobile RAG systems exhibit significantly high response latency. To address this issue, one promising approach is to reuse intermediate computational results across different queries to eliminate redundant computation. But most existing approaches, such as key-value (KV) cache reuse and semantic cache reuse, are designed for cloud settings and perform poorly on mobile devices as they overlook the distinctive characteristics of mobile RAG. We propose PerCache, a novel hierarchical cache framework designed for reducing end-to-end latency of personalized RAG applications on mobile platforms. PerCache adopts a hierarchical architecture that progressively matches similar queries and query-key-value (QKV) cache to maximize the reuse of intermediate results at different computing stages. To improve cache hit rate, PerCache applies a predictive method to populate the cache with queries that are likely to be raised in the future. In addition, PerCache can adapt its configurations to dynamic system loads, aiming to maximize caching utility with constrained resource consumption. We implement PerCache on top of an existing mobile LLM inference engine and deploy it on commodity mobile phones. Extensive evaluations show that PerCache achieves the lowest average end-to-end latency across five datasets and two LLM architectures, reducing latency by up to 63.5% over the strongest baseline while maintaining comparable answer quality.

Container scheduling.title: DisaggKD: Efficient Knowledge Distillation through Teacher-Student Disaggregation and a Fused Loss
Container scheduling.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) frameworks place teacher and student on the same GPUs, so per-GPU memory limits the teachers that fit. DisaggKD separates them across nodes: teacher replicas stream hidden states to the student, a KD loss over row windows and vocabulary shards equals the full-vocabulary loss in exact arithmetic without forming the full-vocabulary logits, and a prefetch ring paces producer and trainer. Closed-form memory and traffic models locate the memory limits of each layout. On the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to 9B pair, the disaggregated layout matches the LM loss of the colocated run with the same loss and is faster than that run; our fused loss also lets a colocated run train on as few nodes at faster speed, while the split is memory efficient when the student spans several nodes. On the larger pairs, colocated runs with a fused loss still run OOM where the split trains, because teacher weights and student states fill the budget.

Container scheduling.title: Purlin: Separating Orchestration from the Datapath of Collectives
Container scheduling.summary: Distributed inference depends on GPU collective communication that must keep pace with evolving hardware and specialized workloads. However, existing works often couple the semantics, orchestration (where and when data moves), and datapath (how data moves) of collective communication. This coupling makes it costly to adopt new hardware mechanisms and customize communication for applications. We present Purlin, a scale-up communication framework that separates these concerns. At the top of Purlin, we specify collectives as a naming of an input and output layout and a copy or reduction operation. In the middle, we introduce a shared orchestration protocol, Stage, Notify, And Consume (SNAC), which derives coordination from these specifications. Below SNAC sits a hardware-specific datapath we call Atom, which implements two key data movement primitives for collectives: copy and reduce. This separation lets us customize collectives and adopt new hardware mechanisms while reusing orchestration via SNAC. We evaluate Purlin on A100, H200, and B200 GPUs. Across seven collectives, Purlin achieves latency speedups of up to 5.14x and bandwidth improvements of up to 4.50x over baselines. Integrated into SGLang, Purlin improves offline LLM serving throughput and interactivity by 1.13x on average and up to 1.37x over baselines. For online LLM inference, Purlin improves interactivity by 1.26x on average and up to 2.85x, with the largest gain occurring under overload. For diffusion image generation, Purlin reduces end-to-end latency by up to 1.13x.

Container scheduling.title: Capacity over TFLOPS: Memory-Centric Deployment of Large Clinical Language Models on Consumer CPUs
Container scheduling.summary: The dominant barrier to running large clinical language models at the point of care is not arithmetic throughput but graphics memory: consumer GPUs cap at 4-16 GB, while the working set of a 27-billion-parameter model in 4-bit precision is 17-25 GB. We argue that the edge node should be treated as capacity-enabled (system RAM) rather than compute-limited (GPU VRAM), and we test this on commodity hardware. Using an INT4 build of a 27B open model as an architecture-faithful stand-in for a 27B medical model, we measure the memory footprint, inference latency, energy, and federated communication cost of a fully CPU-based pipeline driven by synthetic Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) prompts. On two independent consumer machines (a desktop-class machine with 67 GB of RAM and a 6 GB GPU, and a mobile workstation with 34 GB of RAM and a 4 GB GPU) the model loads entirely into system RAM (37% and 60% utilization, respectively) while both GPUs are out-of-memory before the first step. Inference runs at overnight-batch speed (0.6-2.4 tokens/s for the 27B model), and federated fine-tuning would transmit only a 22.6 MB low-rank adapter, a 99.96% reduction over full weights. The capacity result is independent of CPU microarchitecture, RAM size, operating system, and GPU. We further identify an open, CPU- and NPU-optimized inference runtime as the natural production path for this approach, indicating a privacy-preserving and broadly deployable route for on-premises clinical AI. All data is synthetic; this is a research artifact and not a medical device.
Container scheduling.comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE 15th International Conference on Consumer Electronics - Berlin (ICCE-Berlin). (c) 2026 IEEE. Code: https://github.com/balkeumlabs/LLM-on-CPU

Container scheduling.title: FLAI Protocol: Decentralized Federated Learning with On-Chain Rewards and sPEG-Based Contribution Scoring
Container scheduling.summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without data centralization but struggles with incentive alignment, accountability, and robustness under heterogeneous non-IID data. Existing decentralized FL (DeFL) systems leverage blockchains for coordination yet face high on-chain overhead, unverifiable self-reports, and weak fairness guarantees. We present the FLAI Protocol, a trusted execution environment (TEE)-backed DeFL framework that integrates enclave-validated aggregation, sparse Peer Evaluation Graph (sPEG) scoring, and on-chain settlement. sPEG incorporates peer-based quality, class coverage, promptness, effort, and reputation into composite contribution scores. The protocol formalizes contribution evaluation and tokenized incentive distribution, ensuring verifiable fairness and resilience against free-riding and collusion. We evaluate FLAI on image, text, and healthcare datasets and demonstrate parity with FedAvg in utility while improving fairness and accountability. A case study in consumer eHealth (aggregating wearable and electronic health record data for real-world evidence generation) illustrates the protocol's applicability to privacy-critical domains where equitable rewards, auditability, and data sovereignty are essential.
Container scheduling.comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Published in Proc. 2026 IEEE International Conference on Consumer Electronics (ICCE). (c) 2026 IEEE

Container scheduling.title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
Container scheduling.summary: Training recipes are tuned by hand for one model, cluster and workload, and every new model, accelerator, framework version or dataset means tuning again. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, yet a configuration can run to completion while it silently changes training. ATTUNE is a single coding agent that tunes any working recipe for the workload and stack at hand, unattended, within a GPU-hour budget the user sets. It diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time, guided by a catalog of lessons from past campaigns, and ships a recipe only if it passes a correctness gate: a configuration check against objective-changing settings and known stack defects, and a convergence check of its loss curve against the baseline's. On four held-out models at 64-128 GPUs, ATTUNE raises mean throughput over the strongest public recipe run on our stack by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B (best campaign 11.9%) and 33.9% on GLM-4.5 (54.7%), whose public recipe was written for H100. It keeps Mixtral-8x22B's recipe, where nothing it finds clears the noise band. Under a common GPU-hour budget it beats OptiCo, Bayesian optimization and random search on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2; on GLM-4.5 its mean gain is more than four times the best alternative's at less than half the GPU-hours, and on both models its tuning pays for itself within a day of training. The gate rejects no legitimate run and catches 16 of 24 faulty runs, missing only ones that barely move the 20-step loss. Ablations tie its best campaigns to one of its search rules: retrying an out-of-memory layout with recomputation. We release ATTUNE's code and TrainingThroughputBench, a leaderboard of the fastest known recipes for MoE models up to 744B parameters on up to 256 GPUs, each with its throughput, cost per million tokens and a passed correctness check, at https://github.com/amazon-science/attune.

Container scheduling.title: CacheSmith: Accurate RAG Serving under Latency SLOs with Adaptive KV Reuse
Container scheduling.summary: This paper presents CacheSmith, a KV cache reuse system for RAG prefill that maximizes quality-gated SLO attainment. While context caching lowers prefill latency by reusing precomputed KV states for retrieved chunks, it misses cross-chunk attention that a full prefill would compute over concatenated inputs. Prior selective recomputation schemes tackle this problem but enforce static, one-size-fits-all configurations that fail to effectively handle request heterogeneity or dynamic latency budgets. CacheSmith decomposes selective recomputation into a three-phase workflow of WarmUp, Probe, and Patch that can be dynamically configured to exploit a wide range of cost-accuracy trade-offs. At serving time, an SLO-aware scheduler in CacheSmith forms batches to mitigate inter-request interference during layer-by-layer prefill, while a budget-aware planner configures recomputation phases across the batch to maximize the number of requests satisfying both generation quality and latency targets. Both components make fast, solver-free decisions over profiled cost-accuracy bands. On four benchmarks across varying arrival rates and burstiness levels, CacheSmith improves quality-gated SLO attainment by up to 27.5%, over four state-of-the-art baselines.

Container scheduling.title: Agency as a New Organizing Abstraction for Computer Science
Container scheduling.summary: Advances in large-scale machine learning have enabled agentic AI systems: persistent, autonomous computational entities that pursue goals, initiate actions, and interact with open environments. These systems are often framed as applications of foundation models. We argue that this framing is incomplete: agency is also a candidate new organizing abstraction for computer science. What is new is not the concept of an agent, nor runtime policy generation per se, but its general-purpose, open-ended form, in which systems can synthesize courses of action from goals, observations, and memory, over tools and environments for which no complete task-specific model was specified in advance. Thus agency becomes a systems-level abstraction as well as an AI modeling concept. Where the process abstraction organizes computation around executing programs, agency organizes it around pursuing goals under bounded resources: a process executes a program; an agent pursues a goal. From this perspective, the recurring failures of deployed agentic systems (runaway resource consumption, behavior redirected by adversarial content, opaque continuous operation) are symptoms of structural abstraction gaps, not isolated engineering defects. We examine these gaps across six dimensions (execution, interfaces, correctness, oversight, coordination, and persistence) and argue that closing them requires coordinated advances in systems,
Container scheduling.comment: An extended version of a paper to appear in Communications of the ACM, November 2026

Container scheduling.title: Computing All-Pairs Shortest Communication Time Paths for Periodically Varying Satellite Networks
Container scheduling.summary: We address the problem of designing an efficient algorithm for computing the all-pairs shortest-time paths in time-varying networks, specifically targeting the dynamic topological characteristics of low earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations. We model such temporal graphs as $G = (V, E_t)$, where $V=\{1, 2,\ldots , n\}$ is the set of $n$ vertices in the graph, and $E_t$ is the set of $M$ time-varying edges considered over a total time window of size $T = Mτ$, $τ$ being the duration of each interval in that time window. For such a network, our algorithm finds the all-pair shortest paths in $O(M^2n^3)$-time. A key advantage of our approach is its computational structure, which mirrors two matrix multiplication steps, first in the forward direction and then in the backward direction. This structure of the algorithm makes it exceptionally suitable for parallelization on SIMD architectures like GPUs, thereby offering a significant speedup over traditional shortest-path algorithms and enabling efficient, network-wide message routing in rapidly changing LEO satellite constellations.

Container scheduling.title: GPU Goldmines: Tunable WebGPU Kernels for Edge LLM Inference
Container scheduling.summary: As demand for LLM inference grows and consumer GPUs grow more capable, edge deployment is becoming increasingly attractive. WebGPU is compelling in this setting because it offers cross-platform portability and browser accessibility. However, these same strengths also make high performance difficult to achieve, as an implementation that performs well in one context may not perform well in another. To address this, we present GPU Goldmines, a framework for specifying, executing, and tuning WebGPU kernels. We instantiate GPU Goldmines with kernels for key LLM building blocks: matrix multiplication, matrix-vector multiplication, and flash attention. We characterize performance across diverse devices, shapes, and browsers, and use the resulting database to accelerate subsequent autotuning and configuration selection. On shapes drawn from Llama and Qwen models, our matrix multiplication kernels outperform ONNX Runtime and llama.cpp WebGPU kernels by 7.0x and 1.41x geometric mean, respectively, and deliver end-to-end improvements of 1.48x in the prefill stage of llama.cpp for chat workloads.
Container scheduling.comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables

Container scheduling.title: Towards Resilience: Slice-Driven Orchestration of Mobile IoMT in 6G-Edge-Continuum
Container scheduling.summary: Emerging healthcare services, such as real-time diagnostics, remote health monitoring and computer-assisted surgery, require stringent Quality of Service (QoS) guarantees while operating under limited and heterogeneous edge resources. Existing Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) orchestration methods primarily focus on communication metrics such as latency and bandwidth, while overlooking edge resource constraints and dynamic adaptation to workload and user mobility. This paper presents a novel resource-slicing-based adaptive orchestration framework that integrates 5G network slicing (NS), resource-aware orchestration, and mobility-aware task offloading into a single adaptive system. IoMT services are assigned to distinct 5G network slices while jointly considering CPU capacity, memory availability and amount of storage, enabling more efficient service placement and execution. In addition, the system supports user mobility and dynamic task offloading to maintain service continuity under changing network conditions. SimPy-based simulation demonstrates that the proposed method enhances service deployment efficiency, reduces request blocking, and improves user acceptance while maintaining reliable performance across diverse IoMT scenarios.
Container scheduling.comment: ISMICT 2026- 20th IEEE International Symposium on Medical Information and Communication Technology, Osaka Japan

Container scheduling.title: Protocol Choices Matter More Than the Aggregation Algorithm: Federated Learning for In-Hospital Mortality Prediction in Care-Unit and Multi-Hospital Federations
Container scheduling.summary: Federated learning allows hospitals to train a shared mortality model without pooling their records, but published comparisons of aggregation strategies rarely control the evaluation protocol. This study compared seven strategies (FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedAdagrad, FedAdam, FedYogi and FedCluster) on two federations built with one pipeline: 12 care units of a hospital in MIMIC-IV and 49 hospitals in eICU-CRD. Each strategy was tuned and selected on validation data by the same rule, and every comparison was repeated across 10 seeds with Friedman and Holm-corrected tests. SCAFFOLD ranked first in both federations (AUC-ROC 0.886 and 0.819) and in 17 of 18 variants, but its margin over the runner-up never exceeded 0.008, and a control sharing its local optimizer attributed most of its margin over FedAvg to drift correction. On the multi-hospital federation, federated training matched centralized training. In the care-unit federation, three protocol choices changed discrimination by more than the choice of strategy did: discharge-coded predictors (+0.038 in AUC-ROC), client-level SMOTE (up to -0.074), and evaluating the last instead of the best validation round (up to -0.084). Platt scaling on validation data repaired the risks distorted by imbalance corrections without loss of discrimination. Studies should therefore fix the protocol before ranking algorithms.
Container scheduling.comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, 10 tables. Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/protocol-choices-federated-mortality-D18F/

Container scheduling.title: The ArborX library: version 2.0
Container scheduling.summary: This paper provides an overview of the 2.0 release of the ArborX library, a performance portable geometric search library based on Kokkos. We describe the major changes in ArborX 2.0 including a new interface for the library to support a wider range of user problems, new search data structures (brute force, distributed), support for user functions to be executed on the results (callbacks), and an expanded set of the supported algorithms (ray tracing, clustering).

Container scheduling.title: MCCL: Measurement-based Collective Communication Library
Container scheduling.summary: Collective communication is a critical performance bottleneck in large-scale distributed training. Existing libraries and synthesis frameworks compute open-loop schedules once, assuming a static topology and peak link capacities. In production, however, persistent gray failures can silently degrade link throughput and latency for hours, causing pre-computed schedules to lose much of their efficiency during execution. In this paper, we present Measurement-based Collective Communication Library (MCCL), a collective communication library that closes the loop between runtime network measurement and dynamic schedule synthesis. MCCL passively measures GPU-to-GPU throughput, detects persistent degradation, re-synthesizes the affected communication-intensive schedules with warm-started synthesizers, and hot-swaps them without interrupting training. We validate the complete loop on a multi-node hardware prototype and use simulations to evaluate cluster-scale scenarios. In our experiments, MCCL incurs negligible overhead (<2%) while maintaining high measurement accuracy (<1.2% error) and low schedule hot-swap time (about 12 ms). Notably, under gray failures, MCCL reduces training time by up to 4.99x over static schedules on simulated training workloads for state-of-the-art LLMs such as Llama and DeepSeek.
Container scheduling.comment: 25 pages, 17 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for publication in Proceedings of the ACM on Networking (PACMNET), Vol. 4, No. CoNEXT4, Article 55, December 2026. DOI: 10.1145/3856969

Container scheduling.title: FlashT2S: GPU-Accelerated Tensor-to-Spike Conversion Operators for Heterogeneous Neuromorphic LLM Backends
Container scheduling.summary:
Artificial intelligence faces two growing challenges: computational bottlenecks and energy inefficiency inherent to the von Neumann architecture. Neuromorphic computing offers a promising alternative, yet its immature ecosystem still relies on conventional systems for data supply, requiring efficient conversion between tensor and spike dataflow.
  We observe a clear mismatch, where data conversion is slow while downstream computation is fast. As data size grows quadratically with large language models, this mismatch becomes a major bottleneck.
  In this work, we examine the data-conversion components that appear on the critical path of training and inference in neuromorphic LLMs. The work presents FlashT2S (Flash Tensor-to-Spike): GPU-Accelerated Tensor-to-Spike Conversion Operators, which applies architecture-aware and data-centric optimizations to reduce conversion latency. Experimental results show that FlashT2S delivers an average speedup of 850.78x over the native operators across individual operators and 802.83x in realistic workloads. Additionally, compared with GPU kernels automatically generated by torch.compile, our kernels achieve 5-11x speedups. Notably, it achieves near-optimal absolute performance: large-scale conversions are reduced to tens of microseconds (10-99 us), while small-scale conversions reach single-digit microsecond levels (less than 10 us). Furthermore, its standardized output enables seamless integration across heterogeneous backends, including diverse neuromorphic hardware.

Container scheduling.title: Mixture of GFlowNets
Container scheduling.summary: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) learn a policy that samples compositional objects in proportion to an unnormalized reward $R(x)$. This makes them useful wherever many diverse, high-reward candidates are needed and oracle queries are expensive. In practice, a single GFlowNet often fails to cover all modes of a complex distribution, and the obvious ways to scale compute saturate: larger batches and data-parallel gradient averaging draw every trajectory from one, possibly biased, policy, so extra rollouts rediscover known modes instead of finding new ones. We explore whether this mode-bias problem (mode collapse in the extreme) can be addressed with a population of asynchronously trained policies which divide the state space between them. Mixture of GFlowNets (MoG) replaces the single forward policy with a community of $K$ independent GFlowNets coupled through one jointly trained soft classifier, which assigns each member its own region of the state space through reward shaping. Mixing the members under their learned partition functions provably recovers the target $p(x)\propto R(x)$. MoG exchange (MoGX) also lets the classifier route sampled trajectories: a trajectory the classifier assigns to another member is sent to that member and trained on there, with no importance sampling. We evaluate both methods by keeping the environment-interaction budget fixed while scaling the community size, turning parallel compute into mode coverage without extra oracle calls. On HyperGrid, across six reward landscapes and communities of up to $K{=}64$, MoG and MoGX keep finding new modes as $K$ grows, while data-parallel training saturates. On a genomic ideotype-design task, MoGX covers $39%$ of the $1024$ optima at $K{=}64$, against $31\%$ for independent agents and $20\%$ for data-parallel training. MoG also has a lower per-iteration synchronization cost than data-parallel training.
Container scheduling.comment: 30 Pages, 21 Figures, 14 Tables, under review. Omar G. Younis and Joseph D. Viviano are co-lead authors

Container scheduling.title: MODAIC: Coordinated Asynchrony for Decentralized Multimodal Learning
Container scheduling.summary: Multimodal decentralized learning enables collaboration across heterogeneous edge devices without sharing raw data, but differing modality sets create coupled computation and communication bottlenecks. Multimodal agents support cross-modal alignment while training more model components and sharing bandwidth across multiple modality overlays. Under bandwidth limits, these agents can become hot spots: transfers miss aggregation windows, and their updates become stale or underrepresented, degrading worst-agent accuracy. Asynchrony removes global blocking but does not by itself coordinate local cross-modal interaction with timely peer-update exchange. We present MODAIC (Modality-Decoupled Asynchrony with Interleaved Coordination), a wait-free system that coordinates local modality progress, peer-to-peer update delivery, and aggregation under heterogeneous compute and bandwidth. Hierarchical asynchrony lets modalities progress independently while enforcing reciprocal feature exchange; load-aware update fetching overlaps training with communication, limits concurrent serving load, and reuses late arrivals; and consensus-aware peer selection uses lightweight metadata to account for update availability, peer participation, and loss similarity without active probing. We implement MODAIC as a containerized multi-agent framework and evaluate it on local and cross-region cloud testbeds. Across AVE and KU-HAR, MODAIC improves average accuracy and multimodal worst-agent performance. On AVE at 200 Mbps per agent, it improves multimodal worst-agent accuracy by 11.0 percentage points at 1000 seconds over the strongest baseline. On the cloud testbed, it reduces time-to-accuracy by up to 30%. Ablations show that simpler load-balancing and delayed-aggregation variants leave a worst-agent accuracy gap, and stress tests show tolerance to WAN variability and partial tracker unavailability.

Container scheduling.title: Beyond the Boundary: Optimal Grid Dispersion by Spread, Reverse, and Collect
Container scheduling.summary: \emph{Dispersion} requires a set of mobile agents to occupy distinct nodes of a graph such that each node contains at most one agent. We study deterministic dispersion of $k\le n$ agents on an $n$-node oriented square grid, where each node has globally consistent North, East, South, and West port labels, from arbitrary initial configurations. This includes both \emph{rooted} configurations, where all agents are co-located initially, and \emph{general} configurations, where agents are initially distributed arbitrarily across the nodes. On oriented square grids, Kshemkalyani, Molla, and Sharma~\cite{KMS20} gave an $O(\min(k,\Side))$-round algorithm in the local-communication model, where only agents on the same node can exchange information, and an $O(\sqrt{k})$-round algorithm in the global-communication model, where any two agents can communicate regardless of position, both using $O(\log k)$ bits per agent. The bound in the local communication model is optimal when $k=Θ(n)$, but it remains open whether local communication alone can match the $Ω(\sqrt{k})$ time lower bound when $k=o(n)$. We solve this by presenting \textsc{Spread--Reverse--Collect} (SRC), a deterministic algorithm that disperses any $k\le n$ agents in $O(\sqrt{k})$ synchronous rounds using $O(\log k)$ bits of persistent memory per agent, matching both time and memory lower bounds. SRC is based on a geometric primitive, a \sharpS-shaped parallel sweep, together with a simple priority rule. Unlike earlier grid algorithms that gather agents at the boundary and spread out from there, each SRC sweep starts from the agents' current position, and when it reaches the boundary the group simply reflects its sweep back inside and continues. SRC therefore needs no knowledge of the grid size and runs unchanged on an infinite oriented grid.

Container scheduling.title: FORGE: Procedural Weight Generation for Sparse MoE Inference
Container scheduling.summary: We introduce FORGE (Fast On-chip Rotor Generation for Experts), a procedural weight generation system for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference. Rather than storing and loading every expert weight tensor from HBM, we show how a compact accelerator inside each Streaming Multiprocessor can regenerate them on-the-fly from $O(\log^2 d)$ rotor parameters per projection. Per replaced layer, gigabytes of stored expert weights are approximated with under a megabyte of seeds. This addresses the dual memory bottleneck of autoregressive Sparse MoE decode, where per-expert FFN operations are HBM-bandwidth-bound at small routed-token counts and the aggregate expert footprint forces multi-node Expert Parallelism (EP) with all-to-all traffic. We realize the approach as the Rotor Generation Unit (RGU), a fixed-function datapath that generates FFN weight tiles without competing with Tensor Core execution. With 30% of the MoE FFN layers replaced across five Sparse MoE models, we estimate 1.3-2.8x higher system throughput at matched GPU count and 1.10-1.15x lower per-user decode latency at short context. In exchange, downstream accuracy on three model families falls below that of the same model fine-tuned without rotor replacement, and the replacement ratio controls this tradeoff. FORGE also expands KV cache capacity by 1.2-2.6x. It is agnostic to the bit width at which weights are stored, so it can compose with quantization. The RGU is fully implemented/verified in SystemVerilog at ~0.9% SM area overhead (0.032 mm^2/SM, 7nm).
Container scheduling.comment: 16 pages. Accepted to ASPLOS 2027

Container scheduling.title: Deploying RDMA for Distributed Inference and Training At Scale
Container scheduling.summary: RDMA can reduce communication overhead in distributed machine learning systems, but realizing these benefits in production requires more than replacing TCP. Variable-size messages, concurrent connections, bursty incasts, and service failures introduce challenges that hardware offload alone cannot address. This paper reports our experience deploying ByteExpress, a software communication layer over hardware RDMA, in ByteDance's parameter-server-based inference and training systems. We present three lessons from the deployment: efficient RDMA requires buffer management across application and transport layers; scalable communication requires coordinated management of connections, receive capacity, and outstanding data; and service availability requires recovery above the transport layer. ByteExpress combines an RDMA-aware allocator, zero-copy transfers, QP multiplexing, receive-credit flow control, a software send window, and RPC-assisted recovery. In production inference, ByteExpress reduces mean and P99 model parameter fetch latency by 35.7% and 43.7%, respectively, and total CPU usage by 10.69% compared with kernel TCP. In training, ByteExpress reduces P99 model parameter push latency by up to 74.0% compared with TCP, with no PFC pauses observed at runtime.
Container scheduling.comment: 14 pages, 16 figures

Container scheduling.title: Efficient Resource-Shiftable RL Post-training with Generative Rewards
Container scheduling.summary:
Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training with generative reward models (GenRM) has become a central recipe for improving large language models (LLMs), and it is also increasingly resource-intensive: policy rollout, GenRM-based reward evaluation, and policy training all compete for GPU resources. However, existing colocated and disaggregated systems rely on static resource allocation for these roles. Such allocation cannot adapt as each role's workload changes during RL and therefore leaves a role's resources underutilized.
  We present PivotRL, an RL post-training system that dynamically shifts resources among different roles according to their runtime demands. PivotRL introduces a resource-shiftable runtime built on a Global Parameter Storage, together with a unified mechanism that efficiently shifts role-specific context. A shift-aware scheduler enables sequence migration upon a shift, while a planner considers the aggregate throughput benefit and the shift overhead to determine when and how to shift. We evaluate PivotRL on a 128-GPU cluster using four model groups spanning dense and mixture-of-experts models. PivotRL enables resource shifting within seconds and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.81-2.05 times over colocated deployment and 1.50-1.95 times over disaggregated deployment, while preserving RL convergence.

Container scheduling.title: Improved Massively Parallel Shortest Path Computation
Container scheduling.summary:
We present new algorithms for approximate shortest path computation in weighted undirected graphs within the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model. Specifically, we construct an $a$-approximate Single-Source Shortest Path (SSSP) oracle: Given a query consisting of a source vertex $u \in V$, the oracle returns $a$-approximate distances $δ(u,v)$ for all $v \in V$.
  Fix an $n$-vertex weighted undirected graph. We consider two regimes of the MPC model: the near-linear regime, where each machine has $\tildeΘ(n)$ memory, and the heterogeneous regime, where all machines have $Θ(n^γ)$ memory for some constant $γ\in (0,1]$, except for a single machine with $\tildeΘ(n)$ memory. We develop randomised algorithms that construct $O(1)$-approximate SSSP oracles in $O(\log\log n)$ rounds in the near-linear regime and in $O(\log^2\log n)$ rounds in the heterogeneous regime. These oracles answer distance queries in $O(1)$ rounds. Our results improve upon the recent work of Dory and Matar (SPAA 2024) which, for the same total memory, requires $\left(\log\log n\right)^{2+O(1/γ)}$ rounds and applies only to unweighted graphs in the heterogeneous setting.
  We say that $\tilde N_k(u)$ is the approximate $k$-nearest neighbourhood of a vertex $u$ if there exists an approximate distance estimate $δ$ such that $\tilde N_k(u)$ consists of the $k$ vertices closest to $u$ according to $δ$, breaking ties by vertex ID. The main technical ingredient is a new method for efficiently computing approximate $n^{O(γ)}$-nearest neighbourhoods in the heterogeneous MPC model in $O(\log^2\log n)$ rounds.

Container scheduling.title: PrivacyGuard: Source-Linked Sanitization and Locally Resolvable PII References for Cloud GUI Agents
Container scheduling.summary: Cloud graphical user interface (GUI) agents send instructions and screenshots to remote planners, exposing personally identifiable information (PII). Existing placeholder defenses mask detected spans and reuse exact strings. Fragmented or changed forms can expose PII or break entity continuity across turns. PrivacyGuard addresses this private reference problem with source-linked sanitization (SAN) and a structured reference lifecycle (REF). SAN reconstructs fragmented or overlapping evidence and rewrites the complete source extent. REF links changed appearances to session entities and supports locally resolvable references without returning raw values to the upload path. In five-turn sessions scored against common gold, PrivacyGuard reduces audited source-value leakage by 33.55\%--82.60\% relative to the closest prior full-pipeline system in all four reader--language combinations. REF raises strict cross-form continuity from 0.04 under exact-value reuse to 0.81. In reference-required Android tasks, verified completion rises from 8/30 and 7/30 to 17/30 and 20/30. On AndroidLab, PrivacyGuard achieves the highest or tied-highest task-success point estimate among protection pipelines for all four planners. On PrivScreen, it reduces fixed-reader field exposure by 62.72\%--62.84\% relative to the same baseline. PrivacyGuard lowers upload exposure while preserving a locally resolvable task path.

Container scheduling.title: StageBreaker: Shifting Video RL Post-Training Scheduling from Stages down to Data Dependencies
Container scheduling.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has emerged as the key paradigm for improving autoregressive video models. Emerging vision-language reward models further strengthen post-training with accurate rewards, but their long chain-of-thought inference substantially raises the associated costs, while the pursuit of long videos prolongs policy training. Despite these rising costs, existing video RL systems still adopt coarse-grained stage-centric execution, which stalls policy training until all reward evaluation finishes, replays every trajectory twice due to a further barrier within policy training, and induces load imbalance across GPUs. To address the challenges, we propose StageBreaker, a fine-grained data-dependency-driven scheduling framework, which schedules the true dataflow of an RL step rather than its stages. Specifically, StageBreaker overlaps policy training with reward evaluation by exploiting reward-separable policy training, and merges the two trajectory replays into one by leveraging loss-independent back-propagation. It further balances GPU load by scheduling computation at the finer granularity. Our evaluation results show that StageBreaker achieves a speedup of up to 1.41$\times$ over stage-centric execution.
Container scheduling.comment: 16 pages, 16 figures

Container scheduling.title: The Voter Model with Opinion Graph
Container scheduling.summary:
We study the \emph{voter model with opinion graph}, a generalization of the standard (pull) voter model that adds a notion of bounded confidence. In this process, we consider a finite set $A$ of $n$ agents. Each agent $u \in A$ has an opinion $x_u \in O$, where we model opinions as vertices in an undirected opinion graph $G = (O,E)$ with $|O|=q$. In each step, an agent $u$ interacts with another agent $v \in A$. In contrast to classical voting, $u$ adopts the opinion $x_v$ if and only if $x_v$ and $x_u$ are neighbors in $G$. The process is stable once all remaining opinions are an independent set in $G$. We analyze two variants of the process: the ordinary EdgeVOG process, which samples a pair of interacting agents uniformly at random from all possible pairs, and the productive EdgeVOG process, which samples only pairs with neighboring opinions in $G$.
  We show the following:
  - For every opinion graph and every initial configuration, ordinary EdgeVOG stabilizes within $O(n^2\log n)$ steps in expectation and with high probability. The expectation bound is asymptotically tight. For the productive EdgeVOG process, the expected stabilization time is exactly the initial number of compatible agent pairs, while $O(n^2\log n)$ steps suffice with high probability.
  - An opinion $i$ with initial support $s_i$ survives with probability at least $p_i:=s_i/(s_i+\sum_{j\in N(i)}s_j)$. Further, let $μ= \sum_{i \in O} p_i$, then we show the probability that less than $(1-δ)μ$ opinions survive is at most $\exp(-δ^2μ/(2(Δ^2+1)))$ for every $0\leqδ\leq1$.
  -If $G$ has maximum degree $Δ$ and every opinion initially has support at most $\hat{s}$, then no opinion ever acquires more than $\tilde{O}(\min\{n,Δ^6\hat{s}\})$ agents with high probability. This yields near-linear stabilization bounds for productive EdgeVOG for a large class of configurations.
Container scheduling.comment: Abstract shortened to comply Arxiv requirements

Container scheduling.title: Prorsa: Unleashing the Potential of Prefill-Decode Disaggregation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
Container scheduling.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used to enhance the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in solving complex multi-turn tasks. During rollout, agentic RL exhibits a workload pattern distinct from that of traditional RL: multi-turn interactions repeatedly introduce prefill requests, causing prefill and decode workloads to coexist throughout rollout. This workload makes prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation, a design widely used for online LLM serving, promising for speeding up agentic RL rollout. This paper shows that PD disaggregation can improve rollout efficiency by (a) mitigating interference among data-parallel attention modules, (b) enabling stage-specific parallelism, and (c) reducing end-to-end trajectory completion time. However, a fixed prefill-decode allocation may fail to sustain these benefits as workload composition varies across tasks and over time. We therefore present Prorsa, an agentic RL framework for prediction-guided prefill-decode resource allocation. Prorsa observes the lifecycle of every trajectory to forecast short-horizon prefill and decode demand. These forecasts then guide worker allocation decisions and trigger role switching of rollout engines, aligning prefill and decode capacity with anticipated workload demand. Across synchronous and asynchronous agentic RL settings, Prorsa achieves end-to-end rollout speedups of 1.11x-4.05x over prefill-decode colocation.

Container scheduling.title: Distributed $(Δ+1)$-Coloring in $O(\sqrtΔ+\log^* n)$ Rounds
Container scheduling.summary: We give a deterministic distributed algorithm for $(Δ+1)$-coloring an $n$-node graph of maximum degree $Δ$ in $O(\sqrtΔ+\log^* n)$ rounds in both the LOCAL and CONGEST models. More generally, $(°+1)$-list coloring with lists from a color space of size $C\geqΔ+1$ can be solved in $O(\sqrtΔ\log(1+C/Δ)+\log^* n)$ rounds; in CONGEST, we assume $C\leq n^{O(1)}$. The algorithm combines Barenboim's polynomial coloring procedure with arbdefective decompositions, degree reduction, and a short family of hash functions. Using the polynomial procedure in the degree-reduction framework already gives an $O(\sqrtΔ\logΔ+\log^* n)$-round algorithm when $C=O(Δ)$. Hashing adapts the color space to the current degree and removes the logarithmic factor. We prove the existence of the hash family by the probabilistic method and compute it by deterministic exhaustive search, using unrestricted local computation. We also give an explicit variant based on lossless expanders that avoids this search and achieves $O(\sqrtΔ+\log^* n)$ rounds for $C=O(Δ)$.

Container scheduling.title: CALIPER: Calibrating HPC/AI Network Simulators
Container scheduling.summary: Network simulation plays an important role in HPC/AI system research by enabling exploration of network architectures, communication strategies, and system configurations at scales that may be impractical to study experimentally. Existing approaches to network simulator calibration and validation lack a principled methodology that combines parameter alignment, constrained inference, and independent validation for collective-centric HPC/AI networks. We present CALIPER, a methodology for systematic calibration and validation of HPC/AI network simulators. CALIPER distinguishes directly observable system parameters from auxiliary parameters which are configured via calibration and constrains the latter to feasible domains consistent with the target system. We evaluate CALIPER's hierarchical, scale-aware calibration and its effects on parameter identifiability and generalization using collective communication benchmarks on a reference system with up to 64-nodes at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre. Validation results show that the calibrated parameter configurations identified by CALIPER predict system performance with less than 5% mean errors across scale-up and scale-out network domains. CALIPER demonstrates that hierarchical, constrained calibration can produce simulator configurations whose predictive accuracy persists beyond the observations used for fitting.

Container scheduling.title: Revisiting Fast Tendermint: An Agreement Violation and Two Repairs
Container scheduling.summary: Fast Tendermint reduces Tendermint's good-case latency to two communication steps for n>=5f+1. We show that its published round-change rule violates Agreement: one Byzantine process suffices for every f>=1, and for f>=2 two Byzantine processes suffice without double signing. The failure occurs when a process advances past a round without recording the value that may have been decided there. The Quint specification that accompanies the protocol does not allow this kind of round skipping and is not affected; the violation lies in the published pseudocode. We present two repairs. Walk requires a process to leave each round on a quorum of that round's precommits and to precommit before leaving. It keeps the recorded valid state and removes the wait after a precommit quorum. Justify carries the evidence needed to accept a proposal in the proposal itself, removing both the recorded valid state and the proposer's synchronization wait. Both satisfy Agreement and Validity under asynchrony and Termination under the partially synchronous gossip model of Tendermint and Fast Tendermint. Both retain proposal timeouts. The main text presents the executions that violate Agreement and explains the two repairs. The appendices provide proofs, a brief comparison with other round-change designs, and an extension to chains.

Container scheduling.title: VibeServe: Can AI Agents Build Bespoke LLM Serving Systems?
Container scheduling.summary: For years, we have built LLM serving systems like any other critical infrastructure, with a single general-purpose stack hand-tuned over many engineer-years to support every model and workload. In this paper, we take the opposite bet and let coding agents automatically synthesize bespoke serving systems for different usage scenarios. We propose VibeServe, the first agentic loop that generates entire LLM serving stacks end-to-end. VibeServe uses an outer loop to plan and track the search over system designs, and an inner loop to implement candidates, check correctness, and measure performance on the target benchmark. In standard serving settings, VibeServe matches vLLM and SGLang on Llama-3.1-8B, and delivers 2.3x the goodput of a tuned SGLang for a 397B MoE model on four AMD MI300As. In five non-standard scenarios, VibeServe outperforms existing systems by exploiting opportunities that generic systems miss, spanning non-standard model architectures, workload knowledge, and hardware-specific optimizations. Together, these results argue that infrastructure software should favor generation-time specialization over runtime generality. Code is available at https://github.com/uw-syfi/vibesys.

Container scheduling.title: Federated Coreset Subsampling for Distributed Memory Banks
Container scheduling.summary: In real-world scenarios, industrial processes can span multiple factories and goods are often produced at multiple sites, leading to a shared yet non-identical distribution of data across locations. To address this, we propose two federated approaches for i) combining existing coresets (Double Subsampling) and ii) creating new coresets (Federated Subsampling) in a distributed anomaly detection setting. In particular, we adapt the memory bank based PatchCore algorithm to a federated setting, resulting in increased cold-start performance, resilience to domain- and sensor-shift, and resilience to unreliable actor participation, a common problem in classical, network based federated learning strategies.

Container scheduling.title: Space AI Infrastructure: Where the Edge Meets the Orbital Cloud
Container scheduling.summary: The fusion of artificial intelligence (AI) and space technologies is extending spaceborne intelligence beyond onboard payloads toward a global infrastructure, here termed Space AI infrastructure (SpaceAI-Infra). Its promise rests on two distinctive advantages of space systems: abundant solar energy in orbit and the global reach of satellite constellations. Realizing this promise hinges on a fundamental systems question: How should satellite constellations be designed and orchestrated to deliver data-center-scale AI services competitive with their terrestrial counterparts? This article develops a roadmap-oriented answer. We first chart the evolution of SpaceAI-Infra through three progressive stages: onboard AI, Space Edge AI, and Space Cloud AI. By revisiting the space-constrained fundamentals for end-to-end token services, we derive enabling design principles and translate them into an integrated space edge--cloud architecture. The communication-centric space edge comprises free-flying LEO constellations that provide user-proximate computing and form the access and backhaul fabric for cloud AI services. Complementing the edge, the computing-centric space cloud comprises formation-flying satellite constellations organized as space data centers in dawn--dusk sun-synchronous orbits. A case study demonstrates that the proposed architecture can support data-center-scale foundation-model inference for millions of concurrent users worldwide.

Container scheduling.title: SP-Allreduce: Symmetric Tree Schedules for Tori and Beyond
Container scheduling.summary:
Allreduce is a fundamental communication primitive in large-scale distributed training, and torus interconnects remain widely deployed in high-performance systems. We introduce SP-allreduce, a new allreduce algorithm for $d$-dimensional tori that exploits the symmetry of the topology and routes only along shortest paths.
  We call an allreduce algorithm \emph{fully bandwidth-optimal} if it incurs no bandwidth overhead, no multihop-induced traffic inflation, and achieves perfect per-round load balance. SP-allreduce is based on a family of carefully symmetrized shortest-path trees that guarantees full bandwidth optimality in the $α$--$β$ model. We prove that it uses the minimum possible number of rounds among all fully bandwidth-optimal allreduce algorithms on $d$-dimensional tori, and therefore the minimum running time in this class. In this sense, SP-allreduce refines Bucket allreduce: it preserves Bucket's key strengths while reducing the number of rounds by a factor of two.
  We further extend our approach to broader symmetric topologies and to communication trees of prescribed depths. Experimentally, the resulting algorithms improve over the best compared state-of-the-art algorithms for tori by up to $1.19\times$ on square tori and $1.65\times$ on rectangular tori across the tested configurations. On HyperX and spine-leaf networks, we demonstrate gains of up to $14.82\times$ and $1.72\times$, respectively, over the best evaluated baselines.

Container scheduling.title: Optimal Transport Aggregation for Distributed Mixture-of-Experts
Container scheduling.summary: This paper considers the setting in which local Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models are fitted independently on distributed datasets and must be combined into a single global MoE model. Weighted averaging the local mixtures, whose experts are not aligned across machines, often yields a large mixture with many experts instead of $K$ and does not provide an estimator of the true model parameters. We propose to reduce this large mixture to a $K$-expert MoE by minimizing an expected transportation divergence, in which the transport plan depends on the covariates. A relaxation of this problem separates the experts from the gating network: the experts are computed by a majorization--minimization algorithm, which decreases the objective monotonically, and the gating network is then fitted to the gates implied by the optimal plan, with an explicit bound on the resulting loss. We show that the aggregated estimator is consistent whenever the local estimators are, without requiring the local models to have the same labeling across machines. The procedure only needs a single one-way communication round. Experiments on simulated and real data show accuracy close to centralized estimation at a fraction of its computation time. Our source code is available at https://github.com/nhat-thien/Distributed-Mixture-Of-Experts.

Container scheduling.title: From Nominal Capacity to Deliverable Compute: Design, Calibration and Validation of the D-PIN SCU Dynamic Metering System
Container scheduling.summary: Nominal chip specifications do not capture the compute deliverable by heterogeneous distributed networks under communication, runtime and verification constraints. We formalize D-PIN Standardized Compute Units (D-PIN SCU) as a dynamic metering system for deliverable compute. The system combines five-dimensional resource normalization with topology-aware and runtime-corrected metering. A cluster-scale Roofline model yields a closed-form communication ridge, while runtime factors describe thermal, fault and load effects. We show that runtime deviations cannot be identified from nominal specifications alone. Uniform re-anchoring preserves relative metering results, and a simplex-constrained calibration algorithm estimates resource weights. The framework couples Proof-of-Physical-Work verification to a no-arbitrage condition for over-claiming and electricity-aware pricing. An end-to-end recomputation on the Zhangjiang Science Gate production node covers ten heterogeneous 8-GPU servers totaling 59.5 D-PIN SCU. Billed throughput of approximately 33,000 D-PIN SCU-hours is consistent with the physical upper bound at 78% utilization over 720 hours. Derived metrics are 3.02 kW per D-PIN SCU at the supply-and-distribution design boundary and 0.26 D-PIN SCU-hours per delivered kWh. Empirically calibrated chip values differ materially from datasheet projections; the published calibration is not independently reproducible from vendor specifications. Validation is limited to one production node, and the originality claim concerns the integrated system rather than the SCU terminology or individual components. The framework provides a basis for scheduling, verification and pricing of deliverable compute in distributed heterogeneous networks.
Container scheduling.comment: 51 pages, including Appendices A-D

Container scheduling.title: HeteroVDiff: Pipelining Video Diffusion across Mobile NPU and GPU with Shared Weights
Container scheduling.summary: Video generation is moving from the cloud to phones for privacy and offline use, and applications often ask for several clips at a time, so on-device video generation is a throughput problem before it is a latency problem. Contemporary mobile SoCs carry both a GPU and a neural processing unit (NPU) on shared DRAM, yet existing on-device video diffusion systems run the denoiser on one engine while the other sits idle or only decodes the finished latent afterwards. Heterogeneous designs built for mobile LLMs do not carry over: they synchronise the two engines at every operator and partition weight tensors between them instead of sharing one stored copy.
